title: A Gaussian-Remainder Hierarchy for Sums of Random Variables with Big-Jump Statistics
abstract: We develop an exact Gaussian-remainder hierarchy for the probability density of the sum of $N$ independent, identically distributed random variables with broad, finite-variance distribution for the summands. The hierarchy separates the Gaussian fixed-point contribution from residual sectors that retain the original single-summand density. For subexponential densities, the first nontrivial truncation yields a simple finite-$N$ approximation that involves one convolution with a Gaussian background and a subtraction that removes Gaussian overcounting. This approximation captures the Gaussian center, the crossover region, and the big-jump tail within a single expression, as demonstrated numerically for stretched-exponential and finite-variance power-law examples. The same first-order approximation reproduces the known asymptotic anomalous rate function for sums of stretched-exponential random variables and also provides an accurate approximation to the corresponding finite-$N$ rate function.
summary: This paper introduces an exact Gaussian-Remainder Hierarchy to accurately approximate the probability density of sums of random variables with heavy tails. By separating the sum into a Gaussian bulk and residual jump contributions, the authors derive a simple first-order formula that captures the entire behavior—center, crossover, and far tail—in one expression. This provides powerful tools for analyzing rare events in complex statistical systems.
main_problem: To develop an accurate method for approximating the probability density function of a sum of many independent, identically distributed random variables, especially in regimes exhibiting complex crossover behavior between Gaussian and rare-event tails.
main_result: The authors introduce an exact Gaussian-remainder hierarchy whose first-order approximation successfully captures the central Gaussian bulk, the crossover region, and the far-tail big-jump statistics simultaneously for various distributions.
method: They utilize a specialized convolution decomposition (Gaussian-Remainder Hierarchy) to separate the sum density into a known Gaussian background contribution and residual terms that capture non-Gaussian features like rare jumps.
model_or_system: The model consists of sums of $N$ independent, identically distributed random variables ($X = \sum x_i$) whose single-summand densities can be subexponential (e.g., stretched-exponential) or follow power laws.
key_observables: Probability density function $P_N(X)$, anomalous large-deviation rate function $I(\xi)$, and the ratio of approximate to exact probabilities ($R_{	ext{app}}$).
important_parameters: The number of summands ($N$), the tail behavior of the summand (subexponential vs. power-law), and the order of approximation used in the hierarchy.
main_assumptions: The method assumes finite variance for the single-summand density to define the Gaussian background, though extensions are discussed for cases where moments diverge.
figures_summary: Figures compare various approximations ($P^{(1)}_N$, $P^{(2)}_N$) against the exact result across logarithmic scales, demonstrating convergence in both bulk and tail regions; rate function plots show finite-$N$ rates converging to the asymptotic anomalous rate function.
paper_structure: The paper develops the Gaussian-Remainder Hierarchy for $P_N(X)$, derives the first-order approximation ($P^{(1)}_N$), demonstrates its accuracy across various distributions (stretched-exponential, power-law), and finally applies this framework to derive and verify the anomalous large-deviation rate function.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the rigorous mathematical machinery developed for approximating complex multi-variable probability distributions is highly relevant for analyzing rare events or non-equilibrium dynamics in quantum systems (e.g., tunneling rates, escape probabilities).
